newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW - Brazil mulls placing reais debt abroad.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Brazil mulls placing reais debt abroad.

text.p: Brazil would consider issuing local currency reais bonds in foreign capital markets if the bonds carried "very long" maturities, Central Bank international affairs director Gustavo Franco said.

"One challenge to address in the fourth year of the (anti-inflation) Real Plan is the extension of maturities on domestic debt. I can surely see a role to play by foreigners in this process," Franco told Reuters in an interview late Monday.
Currently, the average maturity on some 245 billion reais ($228 billion) in locally issued Central Bank bonds and National Treasury notes is six months.

While the short-term bonds still offer attractive real yields of up to 13 percent a year, foreign investors have been discouraged from buying them because of financial transaction taxes levied on local fixed-income investments.
Franco said investment banks, representing foreign investors, recently approached the Central Bank to request that it offer reais-denominated debt abroad so investors could avoid the tax.
"They wanted us to offer the same deal to the same investors at the same rates without the tax and we said no. We are interested primarily in investments that are longer term," Franco said.
But Franco said Brazil should not turn away from the strong interest foreign investors have shown in local currency bonds.

"It is important that we exploit the appetite that foreign investors display for running local risk. Suppose we want to sell very long (maturity) local bonds, we may be interested in offering those bonds to foreigners," Franco said.
He refused, however, to say what the Central Bank would consider as a minimum maturity for such a bond.
The Republic of Brazil has been active this year in the Eurobond market, issuing in U.S. dollars, Deutsche marks, Italian lire, French francs, Austrian schillings and Dutch guilder.
Brazil also completed a shelf registration in the United States which will allow it to issue up to $5 billion in Yankee bonds.
Franco said Brazil may consider doing a Yankee issue some time in the second semester, although he ruled out doing a deal during the slow U.S. summer season from June through August.
Brazil's busy foreign bond calendar this year has given Franco an opportunity to meet with European and U.S. investors on a number of bond roadshows.
As a sign of growing foreign confidence in Brazil, Franco said investors no longer question him about details of the government's macroeconomic plan.
"Now they are much more interested in details about the bond and how it is structured," he said.
